derivations.reasoning: The three exponents add to (p^3+q^3+r^3)/(pqr). With p+q+r=0 the identity p^3+q^3+r^3=3pqr applies, so the sum of exponents is 3pqr/(pqr)=3. Confirmed symbolically by substituting r=-p-q (simplifies to 3) and on three numeric triples (2,5,-7), (7,-3,-4) and (1/3,4/7,-19/21), each giving exactly 3.
derivations.solution: Adding the exponents gives \( \dfrac{p^{2}}{qr}+\dfrac{q^{2}}{rp}+\dfrac{r^{2}}{pq}=\dfrac{p^{3}+q^{3}+r^{3}}{pqr} \). Since \( p+q+r=0 \), the identity \( p^{3}+q^{3}+r^{3}=3pqr \) holds, so the exponents total \( 3 \). The product is therefore \( z^{3} \).

derivations.reasoning: An identity in x forces every coefficient to vanish. k^2-5k+4=0 gives k=1 or 4; k^2-3k-4=0 gives k=4 or -1; k^2-4k=0 gives k=0 or 4. The only value common to all three sets is k=4.
derivations.solution: The expression is an identity only if each of its coefficients is zero. From \( k^{2}-5k+4=0 \) we get \( k=1 \) or \( k=4 \); from \( k^{2}-3k-4=0 \) we get \( k=4 \) or \( k=-1 \); from \( k^{2}-4k=0 \) we get \( k=0 \) or \( k=4 \). The single value satisfying all three conditions is \( k=4 \).

derivations.reasoning: Put each equal ratio equal to t. Adding all numerators over all denominators gives (a^2+b^2+c^2) = 2t(a^2+b^2+c^2), so t=1/2 and hence 2a^2=b^2+c^2, 2b^2=c^2+a^2, 2c^2=a^2+b^2. These force a^2=b^2=c^2 (sympy returns b=a, c=a as the only positive solution). Then a^4+b^4+c^4=3a^4 and a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2=3a^4, so the required multiple is 1.
derivations.solution: Let each of the equal ratios be \( t \). Adding the numerators and the denominators gives \( a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=2t\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \), so \( t=\tfrac{1}{2} \) and therefore \( 2a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2} \), \( 2b^{2}=c^{2}+a^{2} \), \( 2c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2} \). Solving these together forces \( a^{2}=b^{2}=c^{2} \). Then \( a^{4}+b^{4}+c^{4}=3a^{4} \) and \( a^{2}b^{2}+b^{2}c^{2}+c^{2}a^{2}=3a^{4} \), so the two expressions are equal.

derivations.reasoning: 1/x = 1/p + 1/q gives x = pq/(p+q). Then (x+p)/(x-p) = -(p+2q)/p and (x+q)/(x-q) = -(q+2p)/q, whose difference is 2(p^2-q^2)/(pq). Multiplying by pq/(p^2-q^2) leaves 2. Confirmed by direct symbolic simplification.
derivations.solution: From \( \dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{1}{p}+\dfrac{1}{q} \) we get \( x=\dfrac{pq}{p+q} \). Substituting, \( \dfrac{x+p}{x-p}=-\dfrac{p+2q}{p} \) and \( \dfrac{x+q}{x-q}=-\dfrac{q+2p}{q} \), so their difference is \( \dfrac{2\left(p^{2}-q^{2}\right)}{pq} \). Multiplying by \( \dfrac{pq}{p^{2}-q^{2}} \) leaves \( 2 \).

derivations.reasoning: Every factor of P (5, 15, 25, 35) is odd, so P is odd; every factor of Q (10, 20, 30, 40) is even, so Q is even. An odd plus an even is odd, and an odd number cannot end in 0. Computed (P+Q) mod 10 = 5.
derivations.solution: Each factor of \( P \) — namely \( 5 \), \( 15 \), \( 25 \) and \( 35 \) — is odd, so \( P \) is odd. Each factor of \( Q \) is even, so \( Q \) is even. Their sum is therefore odd, and an odd number can never end in \( 0 \), so the count of trailing zeros is zero.

derivations.reasoning: If (x-5) is a common factor then x=5 is a root of both. From 25-5-p=0, p=20; from 25-5q-10=0, q=3. Hence p+q=23.
derivations.solution: Since \( (x-5) \) divides both polynomials, \( x=5 \) is a root of each. Substituting into \( x^{2}-x-p \) gives \( 25-5-p=0 \), so \( p=20 \); substituting into \( x^{2}-qx-10 \) gives \( 25-5q-10=0 \), so \( q=3 \). Therefore \( p+q=23 \).

derivations.reasoning: Using p(x)q(x) = LCM x HCF: q(x) = (x+a)(x^3-a^3)(x^2-ax+a^2) / (x^4+a^2x^2+a^4). Since x^4+a^2x^2+a^4 = (x^2+ax+a^2)(x^2-ax+a^2) and x^3-a^3 = (x-a)(x^2+ax+a^2), this cancels to (x+a)(x-a) = x^2-a^2. NOTE the paper is internally inconsistent as printed: the stated HCF x^2-ax+a^2 does not divide the stated LCM (polynomial remainder 2a^3(-a-x)), and p(x) does not divide the stated LCM either, so no genuine pair of polynomials has these as their HCF and LCM. Solved as printed. The product rule nonetheless fixes deg q = 6 - 4 = 2, and C is the only option of degree 2, so no other option is defensible.
derivations.solution: Using \( p(x)\,q(x)=\text{LCM}\times\text{HCF} \) together with \( x^{4}+a^{2}x^{2}+a^{4}=\left(x^{2}+ax+a^{2}\right)\left(x^{2}-ax+a^{2}\right) \) and \( x^{3}-a^{3}=(x-a)\left(x^{2}+ax+a^{2}\right) \), dividing \( (x+a)\left(x^{3}-a^{3}\right)\left(x^{2}-ax+a^{2}\right) \) by \( p(x) \) leaves \( (x+a)(x-a)=x^{2}-a^{2} \). The printed data is itself inconsistent — the given HCF is not a factor of the given LCM, so no actual pair of polynomials can have both — but the product rule still forces \( q(x) \) to have degree \( 2 \), and \( x^{2}-a^{2} \) is the only such choice offered.

derivations.reasoning: Substituting the roots: at x=1 both polynomials give 0, so (x-1) divides both. At x=-1 the first gives 8 and the second -4, so (x+1) divides neither. At x=-2 the first gives 12 (the second gives 0), so (x+2) divides only the second. Hence I alone.
derivations.solution: Testing the root of each factor: at \( x=1 \) both \( x^{3}+2x^{2}-5x+2 \) and \( x^{3}+4x^{2}+x-6 \) vanish, so \( x-1 \) divides both. At \( x=-1 \) they give \( 8 \) and \( -4 \), so \( x+1 \) divides neither. At \( x=-2 \) the first gives \( 12 \), so \( x+2 \) fails even though it divides the second. Only \( x-1 \) works.

derivations.reasoning: Taking one unit of work: 8M+24W=1 and 12M+18W=1 give 6W=4M, so M=1/24 and W=1/36 of the work per day. Then 24 men and 72 women do 24(1/24)+72(1/36)=1+2=3 units per day, i.e. the work takes 1/3 of a day.
derivations.solution: Let one man's daily work be \( M \) and one woman's be \( W \), with the whole job as one unit. Then \( 8M+24W=1 \) and \( 12M+18W=1 \), which give \( M=\tfrac{1}{24} \) and \( W=\tfrac{1}{36} \). Together \( 24 \) men and \( 72 \) women do \( 24\left(\tfrac{1}{24}\right)+72\left(\tfrac{1}{36}\right)=3 \) units in a day, so the job takes \( \tfrac{1}{3} \) of a day.

derivations.reasoning: Writing the pair as kx-5y+6=0 and -12x+4(k-1)y+3=0, the no-solution condition needs k/(-12) = -5/(4(k-1)), i.e. 4k(k-1)=60, so k^2-k-15=0 and k=(1 +/- sqrt(61))/2. The discriminant 61 is not a perfect square, so no integral k exists.
derivations.solution: For no solution the coefficients of \( x \) and \( y \) must be proportional, so \( \dfrac{k}{-12}=\dfrac{-5}{4(k-1)} \), giving \( 4k(k-1)=60 \) and hence \( k^{2}-k-15=0 \). Its roots are \( k=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{61}}{2} \), which are irrational because \( 61 \) is not a perfect square. No integral value of \( k \) therefore exists.

derivations.reasoning: With digits a (tens) and b (units), 7(10a+b)=4(10b+a) gives 66a=33b, so b=2a. With a from 1 to 9 and b at most 9, a can be 1, 2, 3 or 4, giving 12, 24, 36, 48. Brute-force scan over all two-digit numbers returns exactly these four.
derivations.solution: Let the number be \( 10a+b \). Then \( 7(10a+b)=4(10b+a) \) reduces to \( 66a=33b \), so \( b=2a \). Since \( b \) is a single digit, \( a \) can only be \( 1, 2, 3 \) or \( 4 \), giving \( 12, 24, 36 \) and \( 48 \) — four such numbers.

derivations.reasoning: Quarterly rate is 12/4 = 3%. Rs 3300 x 1.03 = Rs 3399 exactly, so one quarter suffices, i.e. 3 months.
derivations.solution: Compounded quarterly at \( 12\% \) per annum, the rate per quarter is \( 3\% \). One quarter turns \( \mathrm{Rs.}\,3300 \) into \( 3300\times1.03=\mathrm{Rs.}\,3399 \), which is exactly the required amount. The time needed is therefore one quarter, or \( 3 \) months.

derivations.reasoning: x = ky. Then x^2+y^2 = (k^2+1)y^2, a constant multiple of y^2, so I is correct. But x^3/y^4 = k^3y^3/y^4 = k^3/y, which varies inversely as y, not directly, so II is wrong.
derivations.solution: Direct variation means \( x=ky \) for a constant \( k \). Then \( x^{2}+y^{2}=\left(k^{2}+1\right)y^{2} \), a fixed multiple of \( y^{2} \), so the first statement holds. However \( \dfrac{x^{3}}{y^{4}}=\dfrac{k^{3}y^{3}}{y^{4}}=\dfrac{k^{3}}{y} \), which varies inversely as \( y \) rather than directly, so the second statement fails.

derivations.reasoning: Daily rates are 1/4 and 1/6. Simulating alternate days: starting with X the job is complete after 14/3 = 4.67 days, i.e. part-way through the fifth day, so I holds. Starting with Y, four days give 5/6 and the remaining 1/6 takes Y exactly one more full day, so the total is exactly 5 days, not less than 5; II fails.
derivations.solution: X does \( \tfrac{1}{4} \) and Y does \( \tfrac{1}{6} \) of the work per day. Starting with X, four days complete \( \tfrac14+\tfrac16+\tfrac14+\tfrac16=\tfrac{5}{6} \), and X finishes the remaining \( \tfrac16 \) in \( \tfrac23 \) of the fifth day, so the first statement is right. Starting with Y, four days also give \( \tfrac{5}{6} \), but the remaining \( \tfrac16 \) takes Y a whole further day, making the total exactly \( 5 \) days rather than less than \( 5 \).

derivations.reasoning: Work is proportional to volume. First wall: 100 x 0.2 x 5 = 100 cubic metres, built in 12 x 8 x 10 = 960 man-hours, i.e. 9.6 man-hours per cubic metre. Second wall: 200 x 0.6 x 5 = 600 cubic metres needs 5760 man-hours; at 16 x 10 = 160 man-hours a day that is 36 days.
derivations.solution: Take the work as proportional to the volume of the wall. The first wall is \( 100\times0.2\times5=100\ \mathrm{m}^{3} \) and takes \( 12\times8\times10=960 \) man-hours, so each cubic metre needs \( 9.6 \) man-hours. The second wall is \( 200\times0.6\times5=600\ \mathrm{m}^{3} \), needing \( 5760 \) man-hours, and \( 16 \) men working \( 10 \) hours a day supply \( 160 \) man-hours daily, so it takes \( 36 \) days.

derivations.reasoning: Let T be the time to the meeting point. P covers the pre-meeting stretch in T and Q covers the same stretch in 1 hour, so 60T = V_Q. Q covers the other stretch in T and P covers it in 4 hours, so 4(60) = V_Q T. Solving gives T=2 and V_Q=120. Confirmed by solving the pair simultaneously.
derivations.solution: Let \( T \) be the time each train travels before they meet. The stretch P covers first is the one Q covers in \( 1 \) hour, so \( 60T=V_{Q} \); the stretch Q covers first is the one P covers in \( 4 \) hours, so \( 4\times60=V_{Q}T \). Dividing gives \( T^{2}=4 \), so \( T=2 \) and \( V_{Q}=120 \) km/h.

derivations.reasoning: In one hour with stoppages the train covers 48 km, which at its running speed of 60 km/h takes 48/60 hour = 48 minutes. The remaining 12 minutes of the hour are spent stopped.
derivations.solution: In one hour of travel with stoppages the train covers \( 48 \) km. At its running speed of \( 60 \) km/h that distance takes \( \dfrac{48}{60} \) hour, or \( 48 \) minutes. The other \( 12 \) minutes of the hour are spent at stops.

derivations.reasoning: Downstream speed x = b + s and upstream speed y = b - s, so b = (x+y)/2 and s = (x-y)/2. The ratio b : s is therefore (x+y) : (x-y).
derivations.solution: If \( b \) is the speed of the boat in still water and \( s \) that of the water, then \( x=b+s \) and \( y=b-s \). Adding and subtracting gives \( b=\dfrac{x+y}{2} \) and \( s=\dfrac{x-y}{2} \). Their ratio is \( \dfrac{x+y}{x-y} \).

derivations.reasoning: Sum of roots is -b and product is c, so c = -b and Q = x^2 + bx - b. I: Q is a perfect square exactly when the discriminant b^2+4b = 0, i.e. b = 0 (giving x^2) or b = -4 (giving (x-2)^2), so 'Q can be a perfect square' is true. II asserts that Q is positive for all real x; this fails at b = 0 (Q(0)=0) and at b = 1 (Q(0) = -1), so as a universal claim it is false. RUNNER-UP: option C, which would win if II were read with the same modal force as I, i.e. as 'Q can be positive for all x' — that is true for any b strictly between -4 and 0. The deliberate contrast between 'can be' in I and 'is' in II is what settles it against C.
derivations.solution: The sum of the roots is \( -b \) and the product is \( c \), so \( c=-b \) and \( Q=x^{2}+bx-b \). It is a perfect square when the discriminant \( b^{2}+4b \) is zero, that is when \( b=0 \) giving \( x^{2} \), or \( b=-4 \) giving \( (x-2)^{2} \); so the first statement is right. The second statement claims positivity for every real \( x \), which fails for instance at \( b=0 \), where \( Q(0)=0 \), and at \( b=1 \), where \( Q(0)=-1 \). Only the first statement is correct.

derivations.reasoning: Let the ages be 4t and 5t. Then (4t-k)/(5t-k) = 1/2 gives 8t-2k = 5t-k, so k = 3t. Ages in complete years force 4t and 5t to be integers, and their difference t is then an integer too. With k = 3t < 10 and k positive, t is 1, 2 or 3, giving k = 3, 6, 9 — three values, each checked to reproduce the 1:2 ratio.
derivations.solution: Write the present ages as \( 4t \) and \( 5t \). Then \( \dfrac{4t-k}{5t-k}=\dfrac{1}{2} \) gives \( 8t-2k=5t-k \), so \( k=3t \). Because both ages are whole numbers, their difference \( t \) is a whole number as well, and \( k=3t<10 \) leaves \( t=1,2,3 \). The possible values \( k=3,6,9 \) — three in all — correspond to age pairs \( (4,5) \), \( (8,10) \) and \( (12,15) \).

derivations.reasoning: 27^27 - 9^40 - 3^79 = 3^81 - 3^80 - 3^79 = 3^79(9 - 3 - 1) = 5 x 3^79. The number is odd and carries no factor 7, so among the naturals below 10 only 1, 3, 5 and 9 divide it. That is four, i.e. more than 3. Confirmed by direct integer computation.
derivations.solution: Writing everything in base \( 3 \), \( 27^{27}-9^{40}-3^{79}=3^{81}-3^{80}-3^{79}=3^{79}(9-3-1)=5\times3^{79} \). This number is odd and has no factor of \( 7 \), so among the natural numbers below \( 10 \) it is divisible only by \( 1 \), \( 3 \), \( 5 \) and \( 9 \). That is four such numbers, which is more than three.

derivations.reasoning: Any common divisor of p and p+q also divides q, and conversely G divides both p and p+q; hence HCF(p, p+q) = G. The identical argument applies to p and p-q. A brute-force check over all pairs with p up to 60 found zero counterexamples to either statement.
derivations.solution: If \( d \) divides both \( p \) and \( p+q \) then \( d \) divides their difference \( q \), so \( d \) divides \( G \); and \( G \) itself divides \( p \) and \( p+q \). Hence the HCF of \( p \) and \( p+q \) is exactly \( G \). The same reasoning applied to \( p \) and \( p-q \) gives \( G \) again, so both statements hold.

Dividing \( p \) by \( 55 \) leaves quotient \( 4 \) and no remainder, so \( p=220 \). Since the product of two numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM, \( pq=44\times4620=203280 \), giving \( q=\dfrac{203280}{220}=924 \). Checking back, \( 220 \) and \( 924 \) do have HCF \( 44 \) and LCM \( 4620 \).

derivations.reasoning: Equal remainders means N divides the differences 631-600=31, 724-631=93 and 724-600=124. Their HCF is 31, and each of 600, 631, 724 leaves remainder 11 on division by 31.
derivations.solution: If the three numbers leave the same remainder on division by \( N \), then \( N \) divides their differences \( 631-600=31 \), \( 724-631=93 \) and \( 724-600=124 \). The greatest such \( N \) is their HCF, which is \( 31 \). Each of \( 600 \), \( 631 \) and \( 724 \) then leaves remainder \( 11 \).

derivations.reasoning: Expressed in thousandths the numbers are 3600, 9 and 270. LCM(3600, 9, 270) = 2^4 x 3^3 x 5^2 = 10800 thousandths = 10.8.
derivations.solution: Scale all three to whole numbers of thousandths: \( 3.6=3600 \), \( 0.009=9 \) and \( 0.27=270 \). Their LCM is \( 2^{4}\times3^{3}\times5^{2}=10800 \). Scaling back down gives \( 10.8 \).

derivations.reasoning: The greatest such speed is the HCF of the two distances. In tenths of a kilometre they are 133 = 7 x 19 and 209 = 11 x 19, so the HCF is 19 tenths = 1.9 km/h, giving times of 7 and 11 hours.
derivations.solution: The speed must divide both distances exactly, so the greatest one is their HCF. In tenths of a kilometre the distances are \( 133=7\times19 \) and \( 209=11\times19 \), so the HCF is \( 19 \) tenths, that is \( 1.9 \) km/h. The journeys then take \( 7 \) hours and \( 11 \) hours.

derivations.reasoning: 256 = 2^8, so the sum of its divisors is 1+2+4+...+256 = 2^9 - 1 = 511. Confirmed by summing the divisors directly.
derivations.solution: Since \( 256=2^{8} \), its divisors are \( 1, 2, 4, \ldots, 256 \). Their sum is the geometric series \( 2^{9}-1=511 \).

derivations.reasoning: Consecutive naturals differ by 1, so any common divisor divides 1 and their HCF is 1 — statement I is correct. Statement II fails at m = 3, n = 5, which are relatively prime but whose product 15 is odd.
derivations.solution: Two consecutive natural numbers differ by \( 1 \), so any common divisor must divide \( 1 \); their HCF is \( 1 \) and they are always co-prime, making the first statement correct. The second fails at \( m=3 \) and \( n=5 \), which are relatively prime yet give the odd product \( 15 \).

The product is a product of odd numbers, so it is odd, and it contains the factor 5^5, so it is a multiple of 5. An odd multiple of 5 ends in 5. Direct computation gives unit digit 5.
derivations.solution: Every factor in the product is odd, so the product is odd. It also contains \( 5^{5} \), so it is a multiple of \( 5 \). A number that is both odd and a multiple of \( 5 \) must end in \( 5 \).

derivations.reasoning: Write N = 2m+1; then N^2 = 4m(m+1)+1, and m(m+1) is even, so N^2 = 8k+1. A scan of all odd N up to 199 gives remainder 1 in every case.
derivations.solution: Write the odd integer as \( N=2m+1 \). Then \( N^{2}=4m^{2}+4m+1=4m(m+1)+1 \), and \( m(m+1) \) is a product of consecutive integers and so is even. Hence \( N^{2} \) is of the form \( 8k+1 \) and the remainder is always \( 1 \).

derivations.reasoning: With original price P, the extra quantity is 2790/(0.9P) - 2790/P = 6.2, which gives 279/(0.9P) = 6.2, so 0.9P = 45. The reduced price is Rs 45 per kilogram (original Rs 50).
derivations.solution: If the original price is \( P \) per kilogram, the reduced price is \( 0.9P \) and the extra quantity bought is \( \dfrac{2790}{0.9P}-\dfrac{2790}{P}=6.2 \). This simplifies to \( \dfrac{279}{0.9P}=6.2 \), so \( 0.9P=45 \). The reduced price is \( \mathrm{Rs.}\,45 \) per kilogram, the original having been \( \mathrm{Rs.}\,50 \).

derivations.reasoning: Successive discounts leave (1 - p/100)(1 - p/200)(1 - p/400) = 0.684. Solving gives p = 20, and indeed 0.8 x 0.9 x 0.95 = 0.684, a single discount of 31.6%.
derivations.solution: Three successive discounts leave a factor \( \left(1-\dfrac{p}{100}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{p}{200}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{p}{400}\right) \), and a single discount of \( 31.6\% \) leaves \( 0.684 \). Setting the two equal and solving gives \( p=20 \), since \( 0.8\times0.9\times0.95=0.684 \).

derivations.reasoning: Speed = 40 - c sqrt(n). At n = 36 the speed is 16, so 40 - 6c = 16 and c = 4. The engine cannot move once 40 - 4 sqrt(n) <= 0, i.e. sqrt(n) >= 10, i.e. n >= 100; a scan over n confirms 100 is the least such value.
derivations.solution: The speed is \( 40-c\sqrt{n} \) for a constant \( c \). With \( 36 \) wagons the speed is \( 16 \), so \( 40-6c=16 \) and \( c=4 \), making the speed \( 40-4\sqrt{n} \). The engine cannot move once this reaches zero, that is when \( \sqrt{n}\ge10 \), so the smallest such number of wagons is \( 100 \).

The two conditions give \( 10(P+1)=7(Q+1) \) and \( 4(P+3)=3(Q+3) \), whose solution is \( P=6 \) and \( Q=9 \). Hence \( x:y=2:3 \), so \( x+y=5 \) and \( x-y=-1 \) in the same units, and \( \dfrac{x+y}{x-y}=-5 \).

derivations.reasoning: Right angle at C gives AC = sqrt(100-64) = 6 cm. P lies on AC produced with AP = 10, so CP = 10 - 6 = 4 cm, and BC remains perpendicular to the line ACP. Hence BP^2 = 8^2 + 4^2 = 80 and BP = 4 sqrt(5) ~ 8.944 cm. The semicircle on AB is incidental to the computation.
derivations.solution: Since the angle at \( C \) is right, \( AC=\sqrt{10^{2}-8^{2}}=6 \) cm. The point \( P \) lies on \( AC \) produced with \( AP=10 \) cm, so \( CP=10-6=4 \) cm, and \( BC \) is still perpendicular to the line through \( A \), \( C \) and \( P \). Therefore \( BP=\sqrt{8^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{80}=4\sqrt{5} \) cm.

derivations.reasoning: There are C(5,3) = 10 groups and each letter appears in C(4,2) = 6 of them. So the aggregate 120 equals 6(A+B+C+D+E), giving a total of 20 and a mean of 20/5 = 4.
derivations.solution: There are \( \binom{5}{3}=10 \) groups, and each of the five numbers appears in \( \binom{4}{2}=6 \) of them. Hence the aggregate of the group sums is \( 6(A+B+C+D+E)=120 \), so the five numbers total \( 20 \). Their arithmetic mean is \( \dfrac{20}{5}=4 \).

derivations.reasoning: Adding a constant to every observation shifts the mean by that constant, so the new mean is 50 + 10 = 60.
derivations.solution: Adding the same constant to every observation increases the total by \( 100\times10=1000 \), so the mean rises by exactly that constant. The new arithmetic mean is \( 50+10=60 \).

derivations.reasoning: Let S be the sum and n the count. Then S - 15n = -90 and S + 3n = 54. Subtracting gives 18n = 144, so n = 8 and S = 30, making the mean 30/8 = 3.75.
derivations.solution: If the numbers total \( S \) and there are \( n \) of them, then \( S-15n=-90 \) and \( S-(-3)n=S+3n=54 \). Subtracting the first from the second gives \( 18n=144 \), so \( n=8 \) and \( S=30 \). The arithmetic mean is \( \dfrac{30}{8}=3.75 \).

derivations.reasoning: With 12 numbers the median is the mean of the sixth and seventh terms, here (8x+1) and (x^2+1). Setting (x^2+8x+2)/2 = 25 gives x^2+8x-48 = 0, so x = 4 or x = -12. Only x = 4 keeps the printed list in descending order (33 and 17 sit correctly between 36 and 13). At x = -12 the entries become -95 and 145, which breaks the stated descending order, and re-sorting that list gives a median of 24.5, not 25. So x = 4 alone.
derivations.solution: There are twelve numbers, so the median is the average of the sixth and seventh, namely \( 8x+1 \) and \( x^{2}+1 \). Setting \( \dfrac{x^{2}+8x+2}{2}=25 \) gives \( x^{2}+8x-48=0 \), so \( x=4 \) or \( x=-12 \). II: tan+sin = sin(1+cos)/cos and tan-sin = sin(1-cos)/cos, so the ratio is (1+cos)/(1-cos); the right side is (cos^2/sin^2)(1+cos)^2/cos^2 = (1+cos)^2/sin^2 = (1+cos)/(1-cos). Both sides identical. sympy simplifies both residuals to exactly 0, and numeric tests at the deliberately non-special angles 17, 41, 73 and 88 degrees give residuals below 1e-160 at 30-digit precision.
derivations.solution: For the first, \( \tan^{4}\theta+\tan^{6}\theta=\tan^{4}\theta\sec^{2}\theta \) and \( \cot^{4}\theta+\cot^{6}\theta=\cot^{4}\theta\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \); since \( \tan^{4}\theta\cot^{4}\theta=1 \), the product is \( \sec^{2}\theta\operatorname{cosec}^{2}\theta \). For the second, \( \tan\theta+\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)}{\cos\theta} \) and \( \tan\theta-\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta(1-\cos\theta)}{\cos\theta} \), so the ratio is \( \dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta} \), which is exactly what \( \cot^{2}\theta(\sec\theta+1)^{2}=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^{2}}{\sin^{2}\theta} \) reduces to. Both are identities.

Triangle \( ABD \) is therefore isosceles and \( \angle ABD=\angle ADB \). Equal arcs also place \( A \) at the midpoint of arc \( BD \), so the radius \( OA \) is perpendicular to the chord \( BD \); as the tangent at \( A \) is perpendicular to \( OA \) too, it is parallel to \( BD \). Both statements are correct.

Since \( 5+2\sqrt{6}=\left(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} \), the edge is \( a=\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3} \) and \( a^{2}=5+2\sqrt{6} \). The total surface area is \( 6a^{2}=6\left(5+2\sqrt{6}\right) \), which is precisely \( 6(x+y) \).

II is pure algebra: with BC = a and BD = d, BC^2+BD^2-DC^2 = a^2+d^2-(a-d)^2 = 2ad = 2 BD x BC, true for any D on BC. Checked exactly on three non-symmetric configurations (apex heights 7, 4, 9 with D at 0.3, 0.7 and 0.25 of the base) and both held with exact fractions.
derivations.solution: Let \( M \) be the foot of the altitude from \( A \); since \( AB=AC \), \( M \) is the midpoint of \( BC \). Then \( AB^{2}-AD^{2}=BM^{2}-MD^{2}=(BM-MD)(BM+MD)=BD\times DC \), so the first statement holds. For the second, writing \( BC=a \) and \( BD=d \) gives \( BC^{2}+BD^{2}-DC^{2}=a^{2}+d^{2}-(a-d)^{2}=2ad=2\,BD\times BC \), which is true for every position of \( D \).

derivations.solution: Because the right angle is at \( B \), the hypotenuse is \( b=CA=\sqrt{a^{2}+c^{2}} \). Computing the area with the legs and again with the hypotenuse and its perpendicular gives \( \tfrac{1}{2}ac=\tfrac{1}{2}bp \), so \( pb=ac \). Dividing by \( b \) gives \( p=\dfrac{ac}{\sqrt{a^{2}+c^{2}}} \), so both statements are correct.

For I, the point P sits at height s on AB, so BP = 2s/sqrt(3) and AP = a - BP = s, making AP : PB = sqrt(3) : 2 ~ 0.866, not 4 : 3 ~ 1.333. So I is wrong.
derivations.solution: Let the triangle have side \( a \) and the square side \( s \), with the square standing on \( BC \). At height \( s \) the triangle is \( a-\dfrac{2s}{\sqrt{3}} \) wide, and setting this equal to \( s \) gives \( \sqrt{3}\,a=(2+\sqrt{3})s \), so the second statement is exactly right. Since \( P \) lies at height \( s \) on \( AB \), \( BP=\dfrac{2s}{\sqrt{3}} \) and \( AP=a-BP=s \), so \( AP:PB=\sqrt{3}:2\approx0.87 \), not \( 4:3 \). Only the second statement holds.

Because \( A \), \( O \) and \( C \) are collinear and \( O \) lies on \( BD \), those distances are in the ratio \( AO:OC=m:n \). Therefore the area of triangle \( BCD \) is \( \dfrac{np}{m} \).

derivations.reasoning: The two triangles do have the same three angles, but not in the order the notation asserts. With A-B-P and D-C-P, the exterior angle of the cyclic quadrilateral gives angle PBC = angle ADC = angle PDA and angle PCB = angle BAD = angle PAD, so the correct correspondence is triangle PAD ~ triangle PCB, with A matching C and D matching B. The notation 'triangle PAD is similar to triangle PBC' asserts angle PAD = angle PBC, which would force angle PAD = angle PDA, i.e. an isosceles special case. Verified numerically on three cyclic quadrilaterals: PAD = PCB and PDA = PBC held every time while PAD = PBC failed every time (85 vs 75, 85 vs 70, 67.5 vs 77.5 degrees). II is true for a trivial reason - both sums equal 180 degrees minus the common angle P - and was confirmed equal in all three cases. RUNNER-UP: option C, which wins if 'similar to' is read loosely as 'these two triangles are similar' without binding the vertex order; the triangles are indeed similar as shapes. Two things push against that reading: the standard textbook statement of this result is written PAD ~ PCB, so writing PBC is a deliberate alteration, and if I were intended to be true then II would be a redundant consequence rather than a statement worth asking about. Confirmed against the printed page: statement I really is written 'PAD is similar to PBC', not the textbook's PCB. One further pointer from the wording itself - statement II asserts the SUM of the two angles rather than the term-by-term equalities. If I held with A matching B and D matching C, then angle PAD = angle PBC and angle PDA = angle PCB would each hold individually and II would be a strictly weaker restatement; the setter writing only the sum is consistent with knowing the term-by-term pairing fails under that labelling.
derivations.solution: Because \( ABCD \) is cyclic and \( P \) lies beyond \( B \) on \( AB \) and beyond \( C \) on \( DC \), the exterior-angle property gives \( \angle PBC=\angle ADC=\angle PDA \) and \( \angle PCB=\angle BAD=\angle PAD \). So the two triangles share all three angles, but \( A \) corresponds to \( C \) and \( D \) to \( B \) — the correct statement is \( \triangle PAD\sim\triangle PCB \), whereas the order written in the first statement would require \( \angle PAD=\angle PBC \), which holds only in an isosceles special case. The second statement is true for every such figure, since both sums equal \( 180^\circ \) minus the common angle at \( P \).

Then AC+BD = (x+y) + (z + xy/z) = (xz+yz+z^2+xy)/z. Verified numerically on three configurations with A and D on the same side of BC on the circle with diameter BC: option B matched to 1e-7 every time and no other option matched. A deliberately wrong construction with A and D on opposite sides (where the segments cannot cross) matched nothing, confirming the check discriminates.

Hence \( \dfrac{AP}{DP}=\dfrac{PB}{PC} \), which gives \( PD=\dfrac{xy}{z} \). Therefore \( AC+BD=(x+y)+\left(z+\dfrac{xy}{z}\right)=\dfrac{xy+yz+zx+z^{2}}{z} \).

So exactly one such cuboid exists.

Hence \( xyz=30=2\times3\times5 \), so \( x=5 \), \( y=3 \), \( z=2 \). The total surface area is \( 2(xy+yz+zx)=2(15+6+10)=62 \) square units.

The area condition \( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^{2}=16\sqrt{3} \) gives \( a=8 \), and the perimeter condition \( 3a=24 \) gives \( a=8 \) as well. Statement II alone says nothing about the angles. Together they rule out the parallelogram, forcing an isosceles trapezium, which is cyclic, so the two opposite angles sum to 180 degrees - confirmed on two trapezia (tops 4 and 2) both giving exactly 180.
derivations.solution: If \( AB \) is parallel to \( DC \) and \( AD=BC \), the quadrilateral is either an isosceles trapezium or a parallelogram. The first statement alone leaves the parallelogram open, and there \( \angle ABC=\angle ADC \) so their sum changes with the shape — for instance \( 126.9^\circ \) or \( 77.3^\circ \).
